summary: PCEP carries path computation requests and answers between clients and path computation elements. This document defines PCEPS, which uses TLS to provide a secure transport for PCEP so the exchanges are protected from eavesdropping and tampering.

plainLanguage.summary: PCEP lets network path-computation systems exchange requests and replies. RFC 8253 defines how those systems start TLS first, so the PCEP conversation can be authenticated and protected.

questions: how to secure pcep with tls
what tls version does pceps require
subtitle: How PCEP peers establish TLS on their existing TCP connection before exchanging PCEP messages.

tldr.problem: PCEP carries path-computation requests and replies, but its original specification did not select a specific mechanism to protect those exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: Peers exchange StartTLS messages after TCP connects, establish TLS with mutual certificate authentication, and then begin the normal PCEP exchange.
tldr.outcome: PCEPS secures PCEP on the existing connection and updates RFC 5440's initialization procedures. RFC 8253 has been updated by RFC 9916.

today: RFC 8253 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5440 and has been updated by RFC 9916.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs a Secure Transport
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) communicate with a Path Computation Element (PCE), and also supports communication between PCEs. The messages can affect network operation and resource allocation. RFC 5440 discusses threats but does not select one protection mechanism.

RFC 8253 defines PCEPS, which uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) as a secure transport for PCEP. The security is provided by the transport and does not change PCEP's own flexibility or extensibility.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP messages can affect how a network computes paths and allocates resources. PCEPS uses TLS to protect those messages while they travel between peers.

sections.title: Starting a PCEPS Session
sections.content:
A PCEPS session starts with a TCP connection. The peers exchange StartTLS messages, negotiate a TLS connection, and then begin sending normal PCEP messages. The StartTLS exchange uses the existing PCEP connection rather than a separate port.

In a TLS session, StartTLS comes before the PCEP Open message. The speaker starts a StartTLSWait timer after TCP is established instead of starting the OpenWait timer. The PCC acts as TLS client and the PCE acts as TLS server.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers agree to use TLS before they exchange ordinary PCEP messages. They use the existing TCP connection for this setup.

sections.title: The StartTLS Message and Failure Handling
sections.content:
A StartTLS message contains only the PCEP common header, with Message-Type set to 13. The PCC requests TLS by sending StartTLS, and the PCE agrees by replying with its own StartTLS. Once both messages have been exchanged, the peers begin TLS negotiation.

If a peer cannot or will not use TLS, it sends a PCErr with Error-Type 25 and an Error-value that describes the failure. A peer that allows both modes must try TLS first; if the other peer indicates that an unsecured session is possible, one retry without TLS may be attempted. If StartTLSWait expires without a suitable message, the speaker reports an error and releases the TCP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each peer sends a StartTLS message before the TLS handshake. If TLS cannot be used, the peers report that outcome and may retry without TLS only when their policies allow it.

sections.title: TLS Requirements and Peer Identity
sections.content:
PCEPS requires TLS 1.2 or later and certificate-based mutual authentication. The negotiated cipher suite must provide integrity protection, and confidentiality is recommended. Implementations must support the cipher suite specified as mandatory in the RFC and must support the mandatory suites for later TLS versions they implement.

The RFC defines two required certificate trust models: certificates validated through a configured certification authority list, or a configured list of trusted certificate fingerprints. In the fingerprint model, implementations must support SHA-256. If TLS negotiation or peer identity verification fails, both peers must immediately close the connection before exchanging PCEP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Both peers present certificates and check the other peer's identity before PCEP begins. If the identity check or TLS setup fails, the connection closes.

sections.title: Compatibility and Upgrades
sections.content:
A PCEP speaker that does not support PCEPS sends Open first. A speaker that supports both secured and unsecured sessions tries StartTLS first and may use the unsecured mode after an error if its local policy permits. A peer that supports TLS only rejects an Open message received first.

An existing PCEP session cannot be upgraded in place; it must be closed and established again with TLS. During an incremental upgrade, implementations should allow secured and unsecured sessions. Once both peers support PCEPS, the RFC says support for unsecured sessions should be removed when the upgrade is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: Older peers can continue to use the original PCEP setup when local policy permits it. To add TLS, the peers close the old session and establish a new one.

sections.title: Security Limits and Status Today
sections.content:
TLS protects message confidentiality and integrity and authenticates peers, but it does not address every threat. The RFC notes that TLS setup costs more computing resources than plain TCP and that accepting unsecured connections can expose peers to downgrade attacks. It recommends strict TLS as the default.

RFC 8253 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5440. Unit metadata lists RFC 9916 as a later update to RFC 8253.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects PCEP messages, but allowing a connection without TLS can let an attacker interfere with the choice. RFC 8253 updates PCEP's original setup rules and has a later update.
